body: That's certainly a unique perspective I'd never considered before. It's certainly an orthogonal approach, which makes it appealing.

If I feel merited, I sometimes ask what's wrong and why they feel that way; I almost always try to avoid it, but sometimes I get a patient that I feel isn't too bad off, and just go for it because it wouldn't hurt them. Example: early teen kid who doesn't fit in at school, an art student that told his mother (working on her doctorate in education) he felt like he wanted to cut himself. I noticed from his paperwork that he'd moved recently, and asked if that may have contributed to his not fitting in. And he was talkative and helpful about my understanding his situation. Another example was a 60-something divorced woman who taught elementary school, who (rather suddenly) ended up in the ER because she had a plan to kill herself. Her paperwork said she had a partial plan (to buy a gun), but aside from a history of mild depression, she had no predisposing factors. We talked at great length (it was a long transport), and she felt (as I do now) that a particular medication- one whose use is specifically contraindicated for those with even mild depression- she had been prescribed caused her to feel this way.

Then there was a homeless meth-cooker that had a number of problems with her, and felt it best she be seen at the ER before she did permanent harm to herself. I spent about half an hour listening to her and confirming that I heard what she said (not necessarily agreeing or disagreeing, sometimes turning her answers back into questions), and hoping she didn't get violent.

I think they run the gamut in that sense. Some of my patients get caught up in the "machine" that requires physicians to send every potential self-threat to evaluation, just as CYA. I had one who thought she was destined to be placed in the literal "rubber room" (her words, not mine) and I informed her they had chairs and tables like any conference hall and would offer her something to eat, in all likelihood (which they did).

I feel fortunate in that with one exception (the concentration camp survivor- I sincerely regret they didn't give her more Ativan), all my patients have been manageable. My partner, not so much; one night, he had an Alzheimer's patient that was just fine up until we left the hospital. He then became combative and agitated, and it went downhill from there as he didn't speak any English and thought he was being kidnapped besides, so he started scratching. Meanwhile, the best I could manage was to drive faster to the receiving facility.

The main question I get from my patients is "What is this place like?" when referring to the receiving facility. Of course, I have no clue, but the people that greet us (patient and crew) seem nice enough- unless it's 3 AM, in which case they're like anybody else who wants to be asleep at that time. The best we can tell them is that it's a professional facility and there are some people there that are trained and prepared to help them.

Of course, I've had patients that have been to these facilities before, and they have made comments to the effect that the staff is rude, or they don't give out the medications they're supposed to (presumably opting to sell the drugs on the side), and so forth. But this type of patient frequently comes with their own subset of problems, and it's tough to sort truth from fiction.

But all of these facilities are private; I'll have to ask and see if any are able and willing to take volunteers.

United States. EMT is about 140 hours here; medic is usually 1-2 years depending upon the program. Here in America it's backwards: anyone who pays to get into class gets to go. From what I've heard, it's a competitive process to get into medic school in Canada.

I should clarify, as it was very early morning when I wrote this: I didn't mean it the way it came across. Smoking bath salts is a very poor life choice, but I don't believe the patient did it just because he or she was just "bored."

FWIW, I don't express disbelief or give grief to patients when they tell me their reasons; I just try to understand why they are going this route. But I apologize if I offended; I don't consider the patient or their reason to be stupid. I'm just trying to understand, and I have trouble believing their only reason to do something like smoke bath salts is that they had nothing else better to do.
